tasks.extracted: 22 studies with 6152 participants (11 to 1837 per study), 57% women, ages 18 to 88, mean age 26.3 (SD 7.9) in the 16 studies reporting it; 10 studies recruited students; no meta-analysis because measures and analyses were too heterogeneous.

tasks.extracted: In the survey of 1837 students, anxiety and depression were the least reported and least severe hangover symptoms, with regret and apathy rated moderately severe; one study found no significant effect on tension-anxiety, and in another the people resistant to hangovers showed no change in depression or anxiety.

tasks.locator: 3.2 Risk of Bias, 3.2.1 Non-Randomised Studies and 3.2.2 Cross-Sectional Studies
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rothman_2026_HangoverNegativeAffectSR.pdf (published version, Drug Alcohol Rev 2026;45:e70052), read in full
tasks.extracted: Almost all non-randomized studies were rated moderate risk of bias (confounding, classification of the exposure, outcome measurement), three serious; none of the cross-sectional studies justified its sample size or dealt with non-response.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rothman_2026_HangoverNegativeAffectSR.pdf (published version, Drug Alcohol Rev 2026;45:e70052), read in full
tasks.extracted: The authors state that the naturalistic designs left the amount drunk, intoxication, tolerance, sleep and pre-existing psychological conditions uncontrolled, and that most studies did not separate low mood due to behaviour while drinking from biological effects of the hangover.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rothman_2026_HangoverNegativeAffectSR.pdf (published version, Drug Alcohol Rev 2026;45:e70052), read in full
tasks.extracted: In all three interview studies, people described sadness, guilt, regret, shame, worry and embarrassment during hangovers, prompted mostly by behaviour while drunk that clashed with their beliefs, catastrophic thinking and a sense of a wasted day; they said that bonding with friends and sharing the unpleasantness of the hangover helped ease these feelings.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rothman_2026_HangoverNegativeAffectSR.pdf (published version, Drug Alcohol Rev 2026;45:e70052), read in full
tasks.extracted: In one cross-sectional survey, depression, anxiety, stress and avoidant coping correlated positively, and mental resilience negatively, with hangover severity; the review gives no coefficients.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rothman_2026_HangoverNegativeAffectSR.pdf (published version, Drug Alcohol Rev 2026;45:e70052), read in full
tasks.extracted: The authors state that intervention studies are needed to test coping strategies and emotion-regulation training against the psychological burden of hangovers.

tasks.extracted: 27 studies, all crossover except two; 37 alcohol conditions, mostly drunk shortly before bed; overall risk of bias low in 6 studies, some concerns in 10 and high in 11 (no washout in five, sleep staging for part of the night or implausibly small variances in five, unclear protocols in three).

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Gardiner_2025_AlcoholSubsequentSleepMA.pdf (journal pre-proof, not the version of record; printed manuscript pages and line numbers), read in full
tasks.extracted: Time in bed was standardized in only two of the studies analysed for REM duration and comparable in two; the authors note that a shorter time in bed after drinking could itself reduce REM sleep, which falls mostly in the second half of the night.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Gardiner_2025_AlcoholSubsequentSleepMA.pdf (journal pre-proof, not the version of record; printed manuscript pages and line numbers), read in full
tasks.extracted: Sleep onset latency did not differ between alcohol and control (-2.0 min, 95% CI -4.3 to 0.2; prediction interval -11.6 to 7.5; k = 34, n = 271; p = 0.074); it was shorter after larger doses (meta-regression k = 30, n = 222; p = 0.004); timing did not moderate it (p = 0.684).

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Gardiner_2025_AlcoholSubsequentSleepMA.pdf (journal pre-proof, not the version of record; printed manuscript pages and line numbers), read in full

tasks.extracted: Re-analysis restricted to the 176 of 307 walkers with a hangover: water drunk during the walk correlated with hangover severity before (r = 0.176, p = 0.019), during (r = 0.243, p < 0.001) and after (r = 0.229, p = 0.002), but not with change in hangover severity (r = 0.103, p = 0.174; r = 0.017, p = 0.828; r = 0.066, p = 0.388).

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mackus_2024_HangoverDehydrationWater.pdf (published version, Alcohol 2024;121:9-18), read in full
tasks.extracted: Water drunk was not correlated with thirst before, during or after the walk (r = -0.028, p = 0.714; r = -0.001, p = 0.993; r = 0.059, p = 0.435) or with changes in thirst (r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046).

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mackus_2024_HangoverDehydrationWater.pdf (published version, Alcohol 2024;121:9-18), read in full
tasks.extracted: After an evening of heavy drinking (amount on the study card), hangover severity was higher than on an alcohol-free day at every hourly rating from 09:30 to 15:30, while thirst was higher only at 09:30 and 10:30.

tasks.locator: The impact of drinking water on hangover severity, 1st and 2nd studies
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mackus_2024_HangoverDehydrationWater.pdf (published version, Alcohol 2024;121:9-18), read in full
tasks.extracted: In a survey of 462 Dutch students water was the most used hangover remedy (55.8%) and was rated 5.8 out of 10 for efficacy while hungover; in a survey of 826 students, water during drinking was rated 5.2 (SD 2.4, N = 618) and water before bed 5.6 (SD 2.6, N = 502); the amount of water was not recorded.

tasks.extracted: The authors note that the 13 publications comprised 10 experimental studies, several more than 40 years old with small samples, and 3 surveys relying on retrospective self-report, and that most studies did not control for food, physical activity or sleep.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Caffeine/Gardiner_2023_CaffeineSubsequentSleepMA..pdf (published version, Sleep Med Rev 2023;69:101764), read in full
tasks.extracted: Caffeine was associated with 45.3 min less total sleep time than control (95% CI 29.0 to 61.5 min; k = 37, n = 340; p < 0.001); meta-regression (k = 30, n = 262) showed significant influences of the timing (p = 0.032) and the amount (p = 0.037) of the final dose, with more loss for larger doses and doses closer to bedtime.

tasks.extracted: Sleep onset latency 9.1 min longer (95% CI 3.8 to 14.4; k = 32, n = 280; p = 0.002); wake after sleep onset 11.8 min longer (2.5 to 21.0; k = 17, n = 148; p = 0.019); sleep efficiency 7.0% lower (4.0 to 10.0; k = 31, n = 274; p < 0.001); REM onset latency unchanged (-1.5 min, -8.1 to 5.2; p = 0.581); none of these moderated by amount or timing.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Caffeine/Gardiner_2023_CaffeineSubsequentSleepMA..pdf (published version, Sleep Med Rev 2023;69:101764), read in full
tasks.extracted: Light sleep (N1) increased by 6.1 min (95% CI 2.3 to 9.9) and 1.7% of the night (0.2 to 3.1); deep sleep (N3 and N4) decreased by 11.4 min (k = 35, n = 127; p = 0.012) and 1.4% of the night (p = 0.028); N2 and REM sleep did not change significantly.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Caffeine/Gardiner_2023_CaffeineSubsequentSleepMA..pdf (published version, Sleep Med Rev 2023;69:101764), read in full
tasks.extracted: 16 of the 20 studies that measured total sleep time found a significant reduction; of the four that did not, two gave caffeine for 9 and 14 consecutive days, and the authors raise tolerance as a possible reason while noting that the evidence for tolerance comes from animal studies.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Caffeine/Gardiner_2023_CaffeineSubsequentSleepMA..pdf (published version, Sleep Med Rev 2023;69:101764), read in full
tasks.extracted: Perceived time to fall asleep was longer with caffeine in 7 of 10 studies and perceived sleep quality lower in 8 of 12, but none of 5 studies found a perceived increase in waking during the night.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Caffeine/Gardiner_2023_CaffeineSubsequentSleepMA..pdf (published version, Sleep Med Rev 2023;69:101764), read in full
tasks.extracted: The authors state that included studies were of healthy adults with low to moderate habitual intake, that too few multi-day studies existed to judge repeated exposure, and that the dose and timing model used only the final dose.

tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Caffeine/Gardiner_2023_CaffeineSubsequentSleepMA..pdf (published version, Sleep Med Rev 2023;69:101764), read in full
tasks.extracted: Risk of bias: 16 studies low, 3 some concerns (no randomized order of conditions) and 5 high (no washout period, or sleep stages reported for only part of the night).
